Direct supplier candidate for AI data-center buildouts because high-density AI clusters increase power, cooling, rack, monitoring, and service complexity.
Central electrical-infrastructure mapping for AI data centers, including power distribution, backup power, switchgear, breakers, transformers, and power-management systems.
AI data-center capacity can be constrained by grid interconnection, substation construction, utility work, and transmission expansion, making Quanta a relevant infrastructure execution candidate.

AI infrastructure semiconductor supplier with exposure to custom accelerators and networking silicon; relevance depends on customer programs, AI revenue mix, and packaging/HBM-like capacity requirements.

AI clusters require high-speed data-center networking; Arista is a key public-market mapping for Ethernet switching exposure, though detailed AI cluster share needs validation.
Less obvious equipment chokepoint candidate because advanced AI packages increase inspection, metrology, and yield-control intensity.
Second-order AI infrastructure candidate if data-center electricity demand drives grid upgrades, dispatchable generation demand, turbine orders, substations, and electrification equipment.

coverage_gaps: The universe is still US-listed and ADR-heavy; later layers should expand to Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Europe, A-shares, and Hong Kong-listed suppliers.
Important non-US HBM and memory mappings remain outside this initial universe, especially SK hynix and Samsung Electronics.

Substrate and packaging-material suppliers are underrepresented; later work should test Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, Nan Ya PCB, Ajinomoto-related ABF exposure, and other advanced substrate/material suppliers.

AI networking is only lightly represented by Arista and Broadcom; later work should map Ethernet switching, optical modules, DSPs, retimers, copper interconnect, CPO, silicon photonics, and related test equipment.
Semiconductor test and back-end equipment coverage is incomplete; later work should include Advantest, Teradyne, Disco, Besi, Camtek, KLA, and other inspection/test/assembly equipment suppliers.
Data-center cooling and power coverage should be expanded to liquid cooling, HVAC, chillers, electrical transformers, switchgear, generators, UPS, busway, and thermal materials.
Utilities, independent power producers, nuclear, natural gas, and renewables are not fully mapped despite AI data-center electricity demand potentially becoming a grid-level constraint.
AI software coverage remains thin; future layers should map data platforms, observability, cybersecurity, copilots, model tooling, inference optimization, RPA, and systems integrators.

This Layer 1C score ranks research relevance only; later layers must add valuation, consensus expectations, revenue exposure, backlog quality, margin sensitivity, customer concentration, and falsification checks.
Primary-source validation is still required for backlog, capex, customer qualification, capacity expansion, product mix, AI revenue materiality, and management commentary.

evidence.claim: TSMC describes its 3DFabric family as including front-end and back-end advanced packaging technologies that support high-performance computing applications, including chip stacking and advanced integration.
evidence.source_title: TSMC 3DFabric Advanced Packaging and 3D Silicon Stacking

evidence.claim: Micron announced volume production of HBM3E and stated that the solution would be part of NVIDIA H200 Tensor Core GPUs, supporting direct HBM exposure to AI accelerators.
evidence.source_title: Micron Begins Volume Production of Industry-Leading HBM3E Solution

evidence.claim: NVIDIA states that its H100 Tensor Core GPU uses HBM3 memory and is designed for AI and high-performance computing workloads.
Vertiv describes itself as a provider of critical digital infrastructure and continuity solutions, including power, cooling, and IT infrastructure for data centers and communication networks.
Eaton describes its data-center offerings as including electrical distribution, backup power, power management, and related infrastructure used in data centers.

The U.S. Department of Energy has identified large power transformers as critical grid components with supply-chain constraints and long lead times, supporting the broader grid-equipment and interconnection bottleneck thesis for AI data-center buildouts.
evidence.source_title: Large Power Transformers and the U.S. Electric Grid

evidence.claim: Broadcom lists networking, broadband, server storage, wireless, and industrial semiconductor products, and has publicly discussed custom silicon and networking products for AI infrastructure in company materials.
ASML states that it supplies lithography systems used by semiconductor manufacturers, including EUV lithography systems for advanced chipmaking.
Arista Networks states that it provides cloud networking solutions for large data-center and cloud environments, including high-speed Ethernet switching platforms.
Onto Innovation lists advanced packaging as a served market for its inspection and metrology solutions, supporting inclusion as a packaging process-control supplier.
Amkor describes 2.5D packaging technology and advanced packaging capabilities, supporting relevance to high-performance compute packaging workflows.
AMD states that its Instinct MI300X accelerator uses HBM3 memory and targets generative AI and HPC workloads.
ASE Technology describes itself as a provider of semiconductor assembly, packaging, and testing services, supporting inclusion as an OSAT mapping for the node.
Microsoft has disclosed substantial capital expenditures related to cloud and AI infrastructure in its financial reporting and investor materials.
Amazon Web Services is a major cloud provider offering machine learning and generative AI services, making it a demand-side participant in AI infrastructure buildout.
Google Cloud offers AI infrastructure, Vertex AI, and related generative AI services, making Alphabet a demand-side and platform participant in AI infrastructure.
Palantir describes its Artificial Intelligence Platform as software for integrating large language models and AI into enterprise and government workflows.

The International Energy Agency reported that data centers, AI, and cryptocurrency could double electricity consumption between 2022 and 2026, with data centers representing a growing electricity demand source.

memory_update.text: Layer 1 AI universe should remain a systems-capacity funnel: hyperscaler and enterprise AI demand flows into accelerators, HBM, advanced packaging, networking, data-center power/cooling, grid interconnection, and software deployment.

Highest-priority AI chokepoint nodes after Layer 1C are advanced packaging/HBM and data-center power/cooling/grid interconnection, with AI networking and semiconductor process control as important follow-up nodes.

Separate demand anchors such as NVDA, AMD, MSFT, AMZN, and GOOGL from bottleneck suppliers such as TSM, MU, VRT, ETN, PWR, ONTO, AMKR, and ASX to avoid confusing AI revenue growth with scarcity capture.
Layer 1C remains too narrow geographically and should be expanded to non-US memory, substrate, OSAT, test equipment, optical networking, power-equipment, and utility/power-generation suppliers.

Later layers must add market-pricing checks, including valuation, consensus revision risk, capex-cycle sensitivity, backlog conversion, margin normalization, and evidence that AI exposure is material to each public company.

summary: Merged Layer 1 AI universe from the Layer 1A theme map and Layer 1B node-level candidate sets. The initial universe is weighted toward Serenity chokepoint relevance: advanced packaging/HBM, AI accelerator demand anchors, semiconductor equipment/process control, data-center power/cooling/grid interconnection, AI networking, cloud demand drivers, and AI software integration. Scores are research-priority scores only and are not investment recommendations.
universe_method: multi-step: theme decomposition -> node expansion -> dedupe/rank
